claim: Two monkeys performed a delayed match to category (DMC) task with high accuracy (monkey A: 91%; monkey B: 97%).
source: Both monkeys performed the DMC task with high accuracy (monkey A: 91%; monkey B: 97%)
evidence: Supported by behavioral performance data from the two monkeys during the task.

claim: Both monkeys achieved greater than 80% accuracy for all 36 stimulus conditions during recordings from each of the three areas.
source: greater than 80% for all 36 stimulus conditions during recordings from each of the three areas (Figure 1C, D, monkey A: PFC = 93% ± 4.6%, LIP = 93% ± 4.8%, MIP = 88% ± 6.3%; monkey B: PFC = 98% ± 1.3%, LIP = 96% ± 4.1%, MIP = 98% ± 2.5%)
evidence: Supported by behavioral performance data across different brain areas and stimulus conditions.

claim: Slightly higher error rates were observed on match compared to nonmatch trials for all three datasets of both monkeys.
source: Slightly higher error rates were observed on match compared to nonmatch trials for all three datasets of both monkeys (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral error rate data referenced in supplementary materials.

claim: Monkeys reliably based their M/NM decisions on the category membership of both sample and test stimuli.
source: These results indicate that monkeys reliably based their M/NM decisions on the category membership of both sample and test stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the high accuracy across different stimulus conditions.

claim: A substantial fraction of neurons in PFC (104/145), LIP (35/53), and MIP (60/66) showed significantly different test-period activity between match and nonmatch trials.
source: In this time period, a substantial fraction of neurons in each cortical area (PFC: 104/145, LIP: 35/53, MIP: 60/66) showed significantly different test-period activity between match and nonmatch trials (match vs. nonmatch; p<0.01, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of neuronal activity data.

claim: PFC showed a relatively balanced distribution of match- and nonmatch-preferring neurons (match:nonmatch, 43:61).
source: PFC showed a relatively balanced distribution of match- and nonmatch-preferring neurons (match:nonmatch, 43:61)
evidence: Supported by classification of neurons based on their response preferences.

claim: LIP and MIP were more biased toward match-preferring neurons (match:nonmatch, LIP: 22:13, MIP: 51:9).
source: while LIP and MIP were more biased toward match-preferringneurons (match:nonmatch, LIP: 22:13, MIP: 51:9, P(PFCvs.LIP) = 0.027, P(PFCvs.MIP) = 5.2 × 10−8, chi-square test)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of neuron distributions across brain areas.

claim: In all three areas, match-preferring neurons exhibited significantly greater activity than nonmatch-preferring neurons during the test period.
source: In all three areas, match-preferring neurons exhibited significantly greater activity than nonmatch-preferring neurons during the test period (P(PFC) = 0.0372; P(MIP) = 0.0427; P(LIP) = 0.012; Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of firing rates between neuron types.

claim: Match-preferring neurons showed significantly greater M/NM selectivity in all three areas compared to nonmatch-preferring neurons.
source: On average, match-preferring neurons showed significantly greater M/NM selectivity in all three areas (P(PFC) = 2.6 × 10−4; P(MIP) = 0.024; P(LIP) = 0.039; Wilcoxon test, Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by unbiased fraction of explained variance analysis.

claim: Match-preferring neurons exhibited significantly shorter-latency M/NM selectivity in PFC than in LIP and MIP.
source: Using an unbiased FEV analysis, we found that match-preferring neurons exhibited significantly shorter-latency (see Materials and methods) M/NM selectivity in PFC than in LIP and MIP (Figure 3A, PFC: n = 40, LIP: n = 22, MIP: n = 50; P(PFC vs. LIP) = 0.026, P(PFC vs. MIP) = 0.0058, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Supported by comparison of M/NM selectivity latencies across brain areas.

claim: The mean amplitude of the LFP in PFC showed significantly shorter-latency M/NM selectivity than in LIP and MIP.
source: The mean amplitude of the LFP in PFC also showed significantly shorter-latency M/NM selectivity than in LIP and MIP (Figure 3C, P(PFC vs. LIP) = 8.9 × 10−4, P(PFC vs. MIP) = 0.014, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Supported by local field potential analysis across brain areas.

claim: PFC neurons showed significantly shorter-latency M/NM selectivity than PPC neurons in a simultaneous recording dataset (p=0.0158).
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, PFC neurons showed significantly shorter-latency M/NM selectivity than PPC neurons in that study (p=0.0158, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Supported by analysis of simultaneous recording data from a different experiment.

claim: The raw LFP amplitude showed shorter-latency M/NM selectivity in PFC than in PPC in 52 of 58 recording sessions from both monkeys.
source: Furthermore, the raw LFP amplitude, which was recorded simultaneously from the two areas, showed shorter-latency M/NM selectivity in PFC than in PPC in 52 of 58 recording sessions from both monkeys (PFC:PPC, monkey Q: 151.2 ms:199.1 ms, monkey W: 157.3 ms:171.7 ms, the difference in 46 sessions reached statistical significance p<0.05, Wilcoxon test; Figure S3D–G).
evidence: Supported by session-by-session comparison of LFP latencies.

claim: Match-preferring neurons in PFC showed greater activity preceding and up to the time of the lever release on match trials compared to nonmatch trials (200–0 ms prior to the hand movement, p=0.0018).
source: Match-preferring neurons in PFC showed greater activity preceding and up to the time of the lever release on match trials compared to nonmatch trials (200–0 ms prior to the hand movement, Figure 4A, p=0.0018, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by analysis of neuronal activity aligned to hand movement.

claim: In LIP, match-preferring neurons showed greater activity during match trials vs. nonmatch trials only prior to, but not coincident with, the hand movement.
source: In LIP, match-preferring neurons showed greater activity during match trials vs. nonmatch trials only prior to, but not coincident with, the hand movement (200–100 ms prior to the hand movement, Figure 4B, p=0.0024; −100–0 ms, p=0.21; paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis of neuronal activity relative to movement.

claim: The activity of match-preferring neurons in MIP during both match and nonmatch trials was very similar both before and during the hand movement (200–0 ms prior to the hand movement, p=0.99).
source: The activity of match-preferring neurons in MIP during both match and nonmatch trials was very similar both before and during the hand movement (200–0 ms prior to the hand movement, Figure 4C, p=0.99, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by comparison of neuronal activity during match and nonmatch trials.

claim: Match-preferring neurons in PFC and LIP are more involved in nonmotor functions during M/NM decisions, such as the comparison of sample and test categories.
source: These results suggest that match-preferring neurons in PFC and LIP are more involved in nonmotor functions during M/NM decisions, such as the comparison of sample and test categories
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of activity relative to hand movements.

claim: Match-preferring neurons in MIP are primarily involved in motor functions such as planning and/or initiating hand/arm movements.
source: while match-preferring neurons in MIP are primarily involved in motor functions such as planning and/or initiating hand/arm movements.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of activity during match and nonmatch trials near movement time.

claim: MIP showed significantly shorter-latency M/NM selectivity in faster vs. slower RT trials (P(FEV) = 0.0011).
source: Both the unbiased FEV and the SVM analyses revealed significantly shorter-latency M/NM selectivity in MIP for faster vs. slower RT trials (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; P(FEV) = 0.0011, paired t-test; P(SVM) < 0.02, bootstrap)
evidence: Supported by analysis of M/NM selectivity as a function of reaction time.

claim: PFC and LIP did not show significantly different M/NM selectivity latencies between faster and slower RT trials.
source: but not in PFC or LIP (Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B; PFC: P(FEV) = 0.20, paired t-test; P(SVM) > 0.3, bootstrap; LIP: P(FEV) = 0.60, paired t-test; P(SVM) > 0.40, bootstrap)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no significant differences.

claim: Test-period activity in LIP showed significantly stronger encoding of both sample and test categories than PFC and MIP.
source: Test-period activity in LIP showed significantly stronger encoding of both sample and test categories than PFC and MIP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, P(LIP vs. PFC, sample) = 0.0083, P(LIP vs. MIP, sample) = 0.00076, P(LIP vs. PFC, test) = 0.0094, P(LIP vs. MIP, test) = 8.3 × 10−6, Wilcoxon test)
evidence: Supported by comparison of category selectivity across brain areas.

claim: LIP is more directly involved in category computation than PFC.
source: consistent with our previous findings (Swaminathan and Freedman, 2012; Swaminathan et al., 2013)—suggesting that LIP is more directly involved in category computation than PFC.
evidence: Inferred from stronger category encoding in LIP and supported by previous studies.

claim: Test-period activity in both PFC and LIP showed a combined encoding of sample and test category information.
source: Meanwhile, test-period activity in both PFC and LIP both showed a combined encoding of sample and test category information, but this was not observed in MIP (Figure 5A–C, PFC: FEV(sam) = 0.0399, p=6.7 × 10−8, FEV(tes) = 0.0108, p=1.7 × 10−5; LIP: FEV(sam) = 0.1143, p=3.5 × 10−6, FEV(tes) = 0.0402, p=5.7 × 10−4; MIP: FEV(sam) = 0.0230, p=3.5 × 10−5, FEV(tes) = 0.0026, p=0.1146; paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA analysis of neuronal activity.

claim: In PFC, there was a significant positive correlation between sample and test category selectivity shortly after test onset (r = 0.38, p=2.9 × 10−6).
source: In PFC, there was a significant positive correlation between sample and test category selectivity shortly after test onset (Figure 5D, r = 0.38, p=2.9 × 10−6, t-test)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of category selectivity.

claim: In LIP, sample and test category selectivity were not correlated (r = 0.086, p=0.54).
source: while in LIP, they were not correlated (Figure 5E, r = 0.086, p=0.54, t-test)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationship.

claim: Neuronal sample category selectivity prior to test onset in PFC but not LIP was correlated with M/NM selectivity during the test period (PFC: r = 0.33, p=6.1 × 10−5; LIP: r = −0.20, p=0.15).
source: Furthermore, neuronal sample category selectivity prior to test onset in PFC but not LIP (−50–50 ms relative to test onset) was correlated with M/NM selectivity during the test period (100–200 ms after test onset) (PFC: r = 0.33, p=6.1 × 10−5; LIP: r = −0.20, p=0.15)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between sample selectivity and M/NM selectivity.

claim: Single neurons in PFC, but not in LIP, integrate sample and test category information.
source: These results suggest that single neurons in PFC, but not in LIP, integrate sample and test category information.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between sample and test selectivity in PFC but not LIP.

claim: LIP showed a positive correlation in test category selectivity between the two sample category conditions shortly following test onset (maximum r = 0.7052, p<0.001).
source: This revealed a positive correlation in LIP shortly following test onset (Figure 6B maximum r = 0.7052, p<0.001, t-test)
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis of test category selectivity.

claim: PFC did not show a strong positive correlation in test category selectivity between the two sample category conditions (maximum r = 0.2472, p=0.0027).
source: but not much in PFC (Figure 6A maximum r = 0.2472, p=0.0027)
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis showing weak correlation.

claim: Decoder accuracy for test category was significantly greater than chance shortly after test onset in LIP (maximum accuracy = 0.7738, p<0.01).
source: As shown in Figure 6C, D, decoder accuracy is significantly greater than chance shortly after test onset in LIP (maximum accuracy = 0.7738, p<0.01, bootstrap)
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis.

claim: Decoder accuracy for test category does not exceed chance in PFC (maximum accuracy = 0.5381, p>0.50).
source: but does not exceed chance in PFC (maximum accuracy = 0.5381, p>0.50, bootstrap)
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis showing chance-level performance.

claim: The combination of sample and test category information during the test period is more consistent with linear integration in LIP compared to PFC.
source: Together, these results suggest that the combination of sample and test category information during the test period is more consistent with linear integration in LIP compared to PFC.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation and above-chance decoding in LIP but not PFC.

claim: The nonlinearity index is significantly greater in PFC than LIP during the early test period (p=0.0093).
source: As shown in Figure 6E, the nonlinearity index is significantly greater in PFC than LIP during the early test period (p=0.0093, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by comparison of nonlinearity indices between brain areas.

claim: Nonlinearly integrating neurons (NINs) showed significantly stronger sample category encoding than either the linearly integrating neurons (LINs) or sample category-selective nonmixed neurons (NMNs) in PFC.
source: Interestingly, NINs showed significantly stronger sample category encoding than either the LINs or sample category-selective NMNs in PFC (Figure 7A, P(NIN vs. LIN) = 0.0036; p(NIN vs. NMN) = 4.6 × 10−8; Wilcoxon test)
evidence: Supported by comparison of sample category selectivity across neuron types.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the degree of nonlinear integrative encoding and the magnitude of sample category selectivity in PFC but not LIP (PFC: r = 0.48, p=1.4 × 10−9; LIP: r = 0.18, p=0.19).
source: This reveled a positive correlation between the degree of nonlinear integrative encoding and the magnitude of sample category selectivity in PFC but not LIP (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A, PFC: r = 0.48, p=1.4 × 10−9; LIP: r = 0.18, p=0.19)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between nonlinearity and sample selectivity.

claim: NINs showed significantly greater and shorter-latency M/NM selectivity than the NMNs in PFC (p(latency) = 8.7 × 10−4, p(magnitude) = 5.6 × 10−4).
source: Furthermore, NINs showed significantly greater and shorter-latency M/NM selectivity than the NMNs in PFC (Figure 7C, E, p(latency) = 8.7 × 10−4, p(magnitude) = 5.6 × 10−4, Wilcoxon test; focusing on M/NM-selective neurons in both groups).
evidence: Supported by comparison of M/NM selectivity between neuron types.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the degree of nonlinear integrative encoding and the magnitude of M/NM encoding (r = 0.75, p=2.0 × 10−27).
source: We found a significant positive correlation between the degree of nonlinear integrative encoding and the magnitude of M/NM encoding (r = 0.75, p=2.0 × 10−27)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between nonlinearity and M/NM selectivity.

claim: There was a significant negative correlation between the degree of nonlinear integrative encoding and the latency of M/NM selectivity of PFC neurons (r = −0.44, p=2.3 × 10−5).
source: as well as a significant negative correlation between the degree of nonlinear integrative encoding and the latency of M/NM selectivity of PFC neurons (r = −0.44, p=2.3 × 10−5)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between nonlinearity and M/NM latency.

claim: The activity of NINs (but not M/NM-selective NMNs) reflected the monkeys' trial-by-trial M/NM decisions (NIN: ROC = 0.604, p=0.0019; PN: ROC = 0.529, p=0.4325).
source: As shown in Figure 7F, significantly elevated ROC values indicate that the activity of NINs (but not M/NM-selective NMNs) reflected the monkeys' trial-by-trial M/NM decisions (NIN: ROC = 0.604, p=0.0019; PN: ROC = 0.529, p=0.4325, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis comparing correct and incorrect trials.

claim: The difference in NIN activity between correct and incorrect match trials was greater than that of M/NM-selective NMNs (p=0.0178).
source: Furthermore, the difference in NIN activity between correct and incorrect match trials (measured by ROC) was greater than that of M/NM-selective NMNs (p=0.0178, Wilcoxon test)
evidence: Supported by comparison of ROC values between neuron types.

claim: PFC nonlinear integrative encoding is a key mechanism for the formation of M/NM decisions.
source: Together, our results suggest that PFC nonlinear integrative encoding is a key mechanism for the formation of M/NM decisions.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between nonlinear encoding and decision-related activity.

claim: 41 of 50 trained RNNs converged to perform the DMC task with high accuracy (99.9% ± 0.0009%).
source: After training, 41 of 50 networks converged to perform the DMC task with high accuracy (99.9% ± 0.0009%), which were therefore included in the following analysis.
evidence: Supported by performance data from trained RNN models.

claim: LIP module units showed significantly greater encoding of both sample and test categories (sample: p=0.0069, tstats = 2.9; test: p=7.6 × 10−24, tstats = 21.8).
source: LIP module units showed significantly greater encoding of both sample and test categories (sample: p=0.0069, tstats = 2.9; test: p=7.6 × 10−24, tstats = 21.8; df = 40, paired t-test)
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNN unit activity.

claim: PFC module units showed significantly greater M/NM encoding (p=1.2 × 10−7, tstats = 6.4).
source: while PFC module units showed significantly greater M/NM encoding (p=1.2 × 10−7, tstats = 6.4, df = 40, paired t-test)
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNN unit activity.

claim: In networks where the M/NM signal emerged late in the LIP module, M/NM selectivity in the PFC module appeared with significantly shorter latency (p=5.9 × 10−9, tstats = 7.9).
source: In particular, in networks where the M/NM signal emerged late (≥100 ms after test onset; n = 17 networks) in the LIP module, M/NM selectivity in the PFC module appeared with significantly shorter latency (Figure 8E; p=5.9 × 10−9 tstats = 7.9, df = 16).
evidence: Supported by latency analysis of RNN module activity.

claim: Sample and test category encoding in the RNNs during the test period was more strongly correlated in the PFC than LIP module (rPFC = 0.34± 0.24, rLIP = −0.15± 0.20, p=2.3e-15).
source: As in the real LIP and PFC data, sample and test category encoding in the RNNs during the test period was more strongly correlated in the PFC than LIP module (rPFC = 0.34± 0.24, rLIP = −0.15± 0.20, p=2.3e-15, tstats = 12.5, df = 40, paired t-test)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of RNN unit activity.

claim: Sample and test information was more nonlinearly integrated in the PFC than the LIP module (p=1.1 × 10−16, tstats = 13.7).
source: and more nonlinearly integrated in the PFC than the LIP module (Figure 8F, p=1.1 × 10−16, tstats = 13.7, df = 40)
evidence: Supported by nonlinearity index analysis of RNN units.

claim: The more-nonlinear units in PFC module showed greater encoding of all the key task variables compared to the less-nonlinear units (sample: p=1.2 × 10−8, tstats = 7.0; test: p=8.9 × 10−18, tstats = 14.8; M/NM: p=1.2 × 10−14, tstats = 11.8).
source: Furthermore, the more-nonlinear units in PFC module showed greater encoding of all the key task variables compared to the less-nonlinear units (Figure 8G, H, sample: p=1.2 × 10−8, tstats = 7.0; test: p=8.9 × 10−18, tstats = 14.8; M/NM: p=1.2 × 10−14, tstats = 11.8, df = 40, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by comparison of task variable encoding between RNN unit types.

claim: In 17/41 networks, inactivating feedback from PFC to LIP during the test period had a significant effect on M/NM encoding in the LIP module.
source: In 17/41 networks, inactivating feedback during the test period had a significant effect on M/NM encoding in the LIP module (Figure 9A, example RNN).
evidence: Supported by in silico inactivation experiments in RNNs.

claim: M/NM encoding in the LIP module at least partially reflects top-down input from the PFC module.
source: These results suggest that M/NM encoding in the LIP module at least partially reflects top-down input from the PFC module.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of PFC inactivation on LIP M/NM encoding.

claim: At every level of inactivation, the more-nonlinear group resulted in a greater behavioral effect than the less-nonlinear group.
source: At every level of inactivation, the more-nonlinear group resulted in a greater behavioral effect than the other group, even though they contained the same number of neurons and were inactivated to the same extent (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by in silico inactivation experiments comparing neuron groups.

claim: Nonlinear integrative units in PFC module play a key role in the M/NM decisions for solving the DMC task.
source: These results suggest that nonlinear integrative units in PFC module of our RNNs play a key role in the M/NM decisions for solving the DMC task.
evidence: Inferred from the greater behavioral impact of inactivating more-nonlinear units.

claim: PFC nonlinear integrative units were more likely to receive greater feedforward input from the LIP module (r = 0.52 ± 0.13).
source: We found that PFC nonlinear integrative units were more likely to receive greater feedforward input from the LIP module, indicated by the positive correlations between the nonlinearity index and the feedforward input weights from the LIP module (Figure 9C, r = 0.52 ± 0.13).
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNN connectivity patterns.

claim: The nonlinear integrative units were more recurrently connected within the PFC module than the other PFC units (input: r = 0.27 ± 0.14; output: r = 0.34 ± 0.14).
source: Meanwhile, the nonlinear integrative units were more recurrently connected within the PFC module than the other PFC units, indicated by the positive correlations between PFC neurons' nonlinearity index and their recurrent input/output weights (Figure 9D, input: r = 0.27 ± 0.14; output: r = 0.34 ± 0.14).
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNN recurrent connectivity.

claim: The nonlinear integrative units in the PFC module were more likely than other PFC module units to project to the match and nonmatch response units (M/NM units: r = 0.30 ± 0.17; fix units: r = −0.20 ± 0.13).
source: Furthermore, the nonlinear integrative units in the PFC module were more likely than other PFC module units to project to the match and nonmatch response units, but not the fixation response unit. This is shown by the positive correlations between the nonlinearity index and the output weights to the M/NM response units, and negative correlations between the nonlinearity index and the output weights to the fixation unit (Figure 9E, M/NM units: r = 0.30 ± 0.17; fix units: r = −0.20 ± 0.13).
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNN output connectivity.

claim: PFC nonlinear integrative units may derive their nonlinear encoding as a result of their hub-like strong interconnection with both input and output units as well as recurrent connections with other PFC module units.
source: These results suggest that PFC nonlinear integrative units may derive their nonlinear encoding as a result of their hub-like strong interconnection with both input and output units as well as recurrent connections with other PFC module units.
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity patterns of nonlinear integrative units.

claim: PFC functions as a candidate source of M/NM decision signals.
source: We found that PFC functions as a candidate source of M/NM decision signals.
evidence: Inferred from the shorter latency and stronger M/NM selectivity in PFC.

claim: LIP's role is more aligned with stimulus evaluation and short-term memory.
source: By contrast, LIP's role is more aligned with stimulus evaluation and short-term memory
evidence: Inferred from the stronger category encoding and linear integration in LIP.

claim: MIP primarily reflects pre-motor/motor functions.
source: and MIP primarily reflects pre-motor/motor functions.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation of MIP activity with hand movements.

claim: Nonlinear mixed encoding of sample and test information in PFC is especially important for mediating the monkeys' M/NM decisions.
source: We also highlight a particular form of encoding in PFC—nonlinear mixed encoding of sample and test information—during the decision phase of the task as being especially important for mediating the monkeys' M/NM decisions.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between nonlinear encoding and decision-related activity.

claim: The shorter latency M/NM selectivity in PFC compared to PPC is consistent with a preferential role for PFC in M/NM decisions.
source: Together, the shorter latency M/NM selectivity in PFC compared with PPC is consistent with a preferential role for PFC in M/NM decisions.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal dynamics of M/NM selectivity across brain areas.

claim: Nonlinear integrative encoding in PFC is a key mechanism for manipulating the encoding of sensory stimuli and items in working memory to form decision-related (M/NM) representations.
source: These results build on and extend previous findings, and suggest that nonlinear integrative encoding in PFC is a key mechanism for manipulating the encoding of sensory stimuli and items in working memory to form decision-related (M/NM) representations.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between nonlinear encoding and M/NM decisions.

claim: In areas closer to sensory input, such as LIP, linear integrative encoding may support independent encoding of visible and remembered stimulus features.
source: in areas closer to sensory input, such as LIP, linear integrative encoding may support independent encoding of visible and remembered stimulus features.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional significance of linear encoding in LIP.

claim: In areas more associated with cognitive or task-related functions, such as PFC, nonlinear mixed selectivity may facilitate the integration of task-relevant variables in order to satisfy the task demands.
source: In areas more associated with cognitive or task-related functions, such as PFC, NMS may facilitate the integration of task-relevant variables in order to satisfy the task demands.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional significance of nonlinear encoding in PFC.

claim: Nonlinear integrative units in the PFC are like 'hubs' with stronger and more widespread connections with input, output, and within-area units.
source: Interestingly, when we compared the patterns of connectivity among RNN units, we found that nonlinear integrative units in the PFC are like 'hubs': in comparison to the other units in the PFC module, they received greater feedforward input from the LIP units, were more recurrently connected within the PFC module, and sent greater output to the two key output units.
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNN connectivity patterns.

claim: Nonlinear integrative units in the PFC module were necessary for mediating the M/NM decisions.
source: Furthermore, through causal inactivation experiments in the RNNs, we showed that the nonlinear integrative units in the PFC module were necessary for mediating the M/NM decisions.
evidence: Supported by in silico inactivation experiments showing behavioral deficits.

claim: Nonlinear integrative encoding, like that observed in PFC, functions as a key neuronal substrate for mediating sequential decisions.
source: Together, our results from both neurophysiological experiments in trained monkeys, and analysis of neural activity and connection weights in trained RNNs, suggest that nonlinear integrative encoding, like that observed in PFC, functions as a key neuronal substrate for mediating sequential decisions.
evidence: Inferred from convergent evidence from neurophysiology and RNN modeling.
